# Local Light Field Fusion

Also called: LFLF, LLFF, Layered Light Field Fusion

## Overview
Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) is a view synthesis method designed for producing photorealistic novel views for well-sampled, forward-facing scenes [S1]. It differs from its siblings by using a trained 3D convolutional network to directly predict a discretized frustum-sampled RGB$\alpha$ grid (Multiplane Image or MPI) for each input view, then rendering novel views by alpha compositing and blending nearby MPIs [S1]. Unlike [Neural Lumigraph Rendering](7369-neural-lumigraph-rendering.md) which optimizes a separate network per scene, LLFF applies a single trained network to predict the MPIs directly from input images [S1].

## How it works
**Inputs:** A set of input images from a forward-facing capture [S1].
**Outputs:** High-resolution novel view images [S1].

**Data Structures:**
*   **MPI (Multiplane Image):** A discretized frustum-sampled RGB$\alpha$ grid representing color and opacity at specific depth intervals within the camera frustum [S1].
*   **3D Convolutional Network:** A trained neural network that takes an input image and outputs the parameters for the MPI planes [S1].

**Steps:**
1.  **Input Preparation:** Collect a set of input images from a forward-facing scene [S1].
2.  **MPI Prediction:** Pass each input image through the trained 3D convolutional network to predict the RGB and $\alpha$ values for the discretized frustum-sampled planes for that specific view [S1].
3.  **Novel View Rendering:** To render a novel viewpoint:
    a. Identify the nearby input views whose predicted MPIs are relevant to the novel viewpoint [S1].
    b. Warp or project the MPIs from these nearby input views into the coordinate system of the novel viewpoint [G].
    c. Perform alpha compositing of the warped MPIs to combine the color and opacity information [S1].
    d. Blend the results from the different MPIs to produce the final image [S1].

**Parameters:**
*   **Disparity Limit:** The method provides a sampling guideline not to exceed 64 pixels of disparity between input views [S1].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
*   **High Disparity:** The method frequently fails to estimate correct geometry in datasets with up to 400-500 pixels of disparity between views, as it exceeds the 64-pixel guideline [S1].
*   **Inconsistency:** Blending between different scene representations (MPIs) for rendering different views can result in perceptually-distracting inconsistency and repeated edges [S1].
*   **Artifacts:** The method exhibits banding artifacts on object edges and ghosting artifacts in complex geometry (e.g., masts, internal structures) [S1].

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** All compared single-scene methods take at least 12 hours to train per scene, whereas LLFF processes a small input dataset in under 10 minutes [S1].
*   **Memory Complexity:** LLFF produces a large 3D voxel grid for every input image, resulting in enormous storage requirements (over 15GB for one "Realistic Synthetic" scene) [S1].
*   **Strengths:** Fast processing time; capable of recovering fine details in geometry and appearance (e.g., non-Lambertian reflectance, fine rigging) for well-sampled forward-facing scenes [S1].
*   **Limitations:** High storage requirements; fails with high disparity (>64 pixels); perceptual inconsistencies due to blending; artifacts like banding and ghosting [S1].
*   **When to use:** When fast processing of well-sampled, forward-facing scenes is required and storage is not a constraint [S1].
*   **When not to use:** For scenes with large baseline disparities, or when storage efficiency and view consistency are critical [S1].

## Background
Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) was introduced as a method for view synthesis, specifically targeting forward-facing captures of real scenes [S1]. It was compared against baselines such as Scene Representation Networks (SRN) and Neural Volumes (NV) [S1]. SRN is limited by selecting only a single depth and color per camera ray, while NV is limited by its explicit 128$^3$ voxel grid [S1]. LLFF was shown to outperform these baselines in qualitative and quantitative metrics for suitable scenes, although it suffered from storage and consistency issues [S1].

## Subtopics

### Neural Lumigraph Rendering
A sibling method that optimizes a separate network per scene. It is chosen when per-scene optimization is feasible and higher view consistency is required than LLFF can provide. See [Neural Lumigraph Rendering](7369-neural-lumigraph-rendering.md).

### Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields
A sibling method focusing on instant rendering capabilities. It is chosen when speed of inference is critical. See [Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields](11565-instant-neural-opacity-light-fields.md).
